title: Drop Missing Data
statement:
LeetCode poses this one in pandas, on a DataFrame named `students`; here the DataFrame is a table and you answer with one MySQL query.

- `students(student_id, name, age)`: one row per student record. `student_id` and `age` are integers and are never null; `name` is text and is missing (`null`) on some rows.

Clean the table by discarding every row whose `name` is missing. Return the remaining rows unchanged, with the columns `student_id`, `name` and `age`. Only a true `null` counts as missing: an empty string or any other text is a real name and its row stays. Rows may come in any order.
constraints: student_id and age are integers and never null
name may be null; only null counts as missing
Every row with a non-null name appears once in the output
reference:
SELECT
  student_id,
  name,
  age
FROM students
WHERE name IS NOT NULL;
brute:
SELECT t.student_id, t.name, t.age
FROM (SELECT student_id, name, age, CASE WHEN name IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS has_name FROM students) AS t
WHERE t.has_name = 1
notes:
## Intuition

In pandas this is `students.dropna(subset=['name'])`: keep a row only when its `name` is present. In SQL a missing value is `NULL`, and the way to test for it is `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. Comparisons such as `name = NULL` or `name <> ''` never answer "true" for a null, so they either drop everything or drop the wrong rows.

## Approach

1. `SELECT` the three columns `student_id`, `name`, `age` unchanged, in the original order.
2. Read them `FROM students`.
3. Keep only rows `WHERE name IS NOT NULL`. No grouping or `DISTINCT`, so repeated rows stay as they are.

## Example 1, step by step

- Student 32 (Piper, 5): `name` is present, kept.
- Student 217: `name` is null, so `name IS NOT NULL` is false and the row is dropped.
- Student 779 (Georgia, 20) and student 849 (Willow, 14): kept.

Three rows remain, exactly the expected output.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) for n rows; one null test per row.
- Space: O(n) for the output in the worst case, when no name is missing.

## Pitfalls

- `WHERE name != NULL` (or `= NULL`) is never true in SQL, so it returns no rows at all; use `IS NOT NULL`.
- `WHERE name <> ''` also drops rows whose name is an empty string, which pandas treats as a real value.
- A string that merely reads `None` is a name, not a missing value; only a true `NULL` is dropped.
- `SELECT DISTINCT` would merge duplicate rows that pandas keeps.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `students` | the input table, read row by row |
| `name IS NOT NULL` | true exactly when the name is present |
| `student_id, name, age` | the output columns, unchanged |

narration.1: Each output row is an input row copied unchanged.
narration.2: Keep the student id as the first column.
narration.3: Keep the name column, which is the one that can be missing.
narration.4: Keep the age column as it is.
narration.6: Drop rows whose name is null; IS NOT NULL is the only test that catches a missing value.
